Applying authorize Per Route →

An Allow-List Middleware Factory

authorize('agent', 'admin') — the same 'a function that returns middleware' shape as validate.js, applied to roles instead of schemas.

authenticate (previous topic) answers "who is this?" — it never asks whether that person is allowed to do what they're trying to do. Those are genuinely two different questions, easy to blur together after Laravel's Auth::attempt()-and-friends handle authentication for you so smoothly that authorization (role/ownership checks) barely felt like a separate concern. authorize.js is exactly the gap between the two:

// Figure 4.9: a role allow-list, as middleware (src/middleware/authorize.js)
export default (...allowedRoles) =>
  (req, res, next) => {
    if (!allowedRoles.includes(req.user.role)) {
      return next(new ApiError(403, 'You do not have permission to perform this action'));
    }

    next();
  };

This is the exact same (a) => (b) => ... factory shape as validate.js (Lesson 3): authorize('agent', 'admin') is called once, at the point a route is defined, and returns a new function — closing over allowedRoles — that Express actually runs per-request. ...allowedRoles (rest parameter syntax) is what lets it accept any number of roles: authorize('customer') for one, authorize('agent', 'admin') for two, with no need for a different function shape depending on how many.

req.user.role is read here with total confidence it already exists — authorize never runs without authenticate (previous topic) having run first on the same router, so req.user is always already set by the time this checks it. A role that isn't in the list gets a 403, not a 401: the caller is authenticated — authenticate already succeeded, or this middleware would never have been reached at all — they're just not allowed to do this particular thing. That distinction is worth holding onto; a later topic this lesson comes back to it directly.
